---
title: "Expressions & Contexts"
subtitle: "≈ data masking · tidy eval: the engine under every dplyr verb"
jupyter: python3
---

Every Polars verb is a **context** that runs **expressions**. Once that pair
is clear, the rest of Polars is vocabulary. This chapter covers what an
expression is, the length rules each context enforces, where output names come
from, and the places where tidyverse intuition gives the wrong answer.

## In tidyverse {#sec-expr-tidyverse}

```r
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins |>
  mutate(
    bill_ratio = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm,
    heavy      = body_mass_g > mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

dplyr does two things here without showing you:

1. **Capture.** `bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm` is not evaluated when R reads
   it. `mutate()` captures the code unevaluated (*data masking*; the captured
   object is a *quosure*).
2. **Evaluate.** `mutate()` then runs that code with the columns of
   `penguins` in scope and attaches the result.

Polars splits these two steps into two things you can see and hold: the
**expression** (step 1) and the **context** (step 2).

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import polars as pl
from pl_notes import datasets

penguins_df = datasets.penguins()   # the same 344 × 8 table as palmerpenguins

penguins_df.with_columns(
    bill_ratio=pl.col("bill_length_mm") / pl.col("bill_depth_mm"),
    heavy=pl.col("body_mass_g") > pl.col("body_mass_g").mean(),
).select("species", "bill_ratio", "heavy").head(3)
```

`.mean()` skips nulls, so `na.rm = TRUE` is already the default.

## Mental model {#sec-expr-model}

```text
 BUILD (plain Python, touches no data)       RUN (a context)
 ─────────────────────────────────────       ──────────────────────────────────────────────
 bill_ratio = (                              penguins_df.with_columns(bill_ratio=bill_ratio)
     pl.col("bill_length_mm")      ───────►  penguins_df.filter(bill_ratio > 2.5)
     / pl.col("bill_depth_mm")               penguins_df.group_by("species").agg(bill_ratio.mean())
 )
 # a pl.Expr: a recipe, not a result         The context decides
                                               • which rows the expression sees  (whole frame / one group)
                                               • which output lengths are legal  (n, 1, or anything)
                                               • what the result becomes         (columns, row mask, row per group)
```

An expression is a function from a frame to a column (`DataFrame → Series`)
that has not been called yet. The context is the caller.

|  | tidyverse | Polars |
|---|---|---|
| Unevaluated column code | captured implicitly (a quosure) | built explicitly: a `pl.Expr` object |
| How it is built | non-standard evaluation captures what you typed | operator overloading: `pl.col("a") / pl.col("b")` calls `Expr.__truediv__`, which returns a bigger tree, not a number |
| Evaluated by | the verb (`mutate`, `filter`, …) | the context (`with_columns`, `filter`, …) |
| Stored and reused with | `quo()` + `!!` or `{{ }}` | an ordinary Python variable |

: Same idea, different mechanism {.striped}

## Mechanics {#sec-expr-mechanics}

### Expressions are values {#sec-expr-values}

Build an expression without any frame in sight:

```{python}
bill_ratio = pl.col("bill_length_mm") / pl.col("bill_depth_mm")
print(type(bill_ratio))
print(bill_ratio)
```

Nothing was computed. It is a tree that names its inputs, and you can inspect
it:

```{python}
bill_ratio.meta.root_names(), bill_ratio.meta.output_name()
```

Remember that output name for later (@sec-expr-naming). The same
expression can now run in any context:

```{python}
penguins_df.filter(bill_ratio > 3.5).select("species", "island", "bill_length_mm")
```

```{python}
penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg(bill_ratio.mean())  # column name: see Naming
```

The R equivalent needs explicit quoting and unquoting:

```r
bill_ratio <- quo(bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm)   # capture
penguins |> filter(!!bill_ratio > 3.5)              # inject
```

In Polars, an expression is already a value: you can keep it in a variable,
put it in a list, or return it from a function, all with no special syntax.
The same expression also works unchanged on a `LazyFrame` (`penguins_df.lazy()`).

### Three output shapes {#sec-expr-shapes}

Every expression maps an input of *n* rows to an output of some length. The
context then checks whether that length is allowed.

```text
 n rows ──► element-wise     ──► n rows    + - * /, abs(), round(), str.*, dt.*,
                                           fill_null(), is_null(), shift(), cum_sum(), rank()
 n rows ──► aggregation      ──► 1 row     mean(), sum(), max(), len(), n_unique(), first()
 n rows ──► length-changing  ──► k rows    filter(), drop_nulls(), unique(), head(k)
```

dplyr has the same three kinds (`x + 1`, `mean(x)`, `x[x > 0]`), and
`mutate()` enforces the same rule: an output must be size *n* or size 1.
Polars enforces a version of that rule in every context except `agg()`:
outputs must share one length, or have length 1 and be broadcast. `agg()`
accepts any length.

### The contexts {#sec-expr-contexts}

| Context | dplyr | Each expression must return | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `select()` | `transmute()`, ungrouped `summarise()` / `reframe()` | one shared length *k*, or 1 (broadcast) | a new frame of *k* rows |
| `with_columns()` | `mutate()` | *n* (the frame height) or 1 (broadcast) | the input plus new or replaced columns |
| `filter()` | `filter()` | Boolean, length *n* or 1 | the rows where the condition is `true` |
| `group_by().agg()` | `summarise()` / `reframe()` | anything: length 1 → a scalar, otherwise → a **list** | one row per group |
| `expr.over(g)` | grouped `mutate()` | group size, or 1 (broadcast within the group) | *n* rows, aligned to the input |

: The four contexts, plus the window {.striped}

#### `select()`: a new frame from expressions

A length-1 result is broadcast to match the others:

```{python}
penguins_df.select(
    pl.col("body_mass_g"),
    avg_mass=pl.col("body_mass_g").mean(),   # 1 value → repeated 344 times
).head(3)
```

All expressions of length *k* is fine. This is dplyr's `reframe()`:

```{python}
penguins_df.select(pl.col("species").unique(maintain_order=True))
```

Mixing two different lengths is an error, not a recycle:

```{python}
#| error: true
penguins_df.select(pl.col("species"), pl.col("body_mass_g").drop_nulls())
```

#### `with_columns()`: add or replace columns

The same rules apply with *k* fixed at the frame height. A length-342
`drop_nulls()` here fails with "can't broadcast Series … of length 342 to
length 344".

```{python}
penguins_df.with_columns(
    bill_ratio=bill_ratio,
    mass_vs_avg=pl.col("body_mass_g") - pl.col("body_mass_g").mean(),
).select("species", "bill_ratio", "mass_vs_avg").head(3)
```

#### `filter()`: keep rows where the condition is true

An aggregation inside the condition is broadcast, as in
`filter(body_mass_g > mean(body_mass_g))`. Comma-separated conditions are
combined with AND:

```{python}
penguins_df.filter(
    pl.col("body_mass_g") > pl.col("body_mass_g").mean(),
    pl.col("island") == "Dream",
).select("species", "island", "body_mass_g")
```

#### `group_by().agg()`: one row per group

`agg()` is the one context that never complains about length. If a result
has more than one row, `agg()` turns it into a **list**:

```{python}
penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg(
    n=pl.len(),                                     # 1 per group → scalar
    avg_mass=pl.col("body_mass_g").mean(),          # 1 per group → scalar
    masses=pl.col("body_mass_g"),                   # n per group → list
    top3=pl.col("body_mass_g").drop_nulls().sort(descending=True).head(3),  # 3 → list
)
```

In dplyr ≥ 1.1, `masses = body_mass_g` inside `summarise()` gives a
deprecation warning and returns several rows per group, which is now
`reframe()`'s job. Polars keeps one row per group and stores the values as a
list column, like `summarise(masses = list(body_mass_g))`.

::: {.callout-tip}
`sort()`, `filter()` and `head()` are applied to a single column here, inside
each group. That is exactly what `agg()` is for. The same calls inside
`select()` can silently misalign rows (@sec-expr-sort-trap).
:::

#### `expr.over(g)`: the window, i.e. grouped `mutate()`

`.over()` is a method on the expression, not the frame: the expression
carries its own grouping, and you run it inside `select()` or
`with_columns()`. An aggregation is broadcast back to the group's rows, and an
element-wise expression is computed separately within each group:

```{python}
penguins_df.select(
    "species",
    "body_mass_g",
    species_avg=pl.col("body_mass_g").mean().over("species"),
    rank_in_species=pl.col("body_mass_g").rank("dense", descending=True).over("species"),
).head(4)
```

The [Window Functions](../transform/window.qmd) chapter covers `order_by=`
and `mapping_strategy=`.

#### Expressions in other arguments

Many verb arguments besides the four contexts also accept expressions. Group by
a computed key (≈ `count(heavy = body_mass_g > 4200)`):

```{python}
penguins_df.group_by(heavy=pl.col("body_mass_g") > 4200).agg(pl.len()).sort("heavy")
```

Sort by a computed value (≈ `arrange(str_length(species), body_mass_g)`):

```{python}
penguins_df.sort(
    pl.col("species").str.len_chars(), "body_mass_g", nulls_last=True
).select("species", "body_mass_g").head(3)
```

`join(left_on=..., right_on=...)` accepts expressions too.

### Naming: where output names come from {#sec-expr-naming}

dplyr names an unnamed output after its code (`mean(x)`). Polars uses these
rules instead:

1. The output name is the name of the **leftmost input** of the expression:
   `pl.col("a") / pl.col("b")` → `a`, and `pl.col("a").mean()` → `a`.
2. An expression that starts without a column gets a fixed name:
   `pl.lit(...)` → `literal` and `pl.len()` → `len`.
3. `pl.when(...).then(...)` takes its name from the first `then()`.
4. Override the name with a keyword argument (`name=expr`) or `.alias("name")`.
   Bulk renames use `.name.suffix()` and similar (see
   [Selectors](selectors.qmd)).
5. Names must be unique within one context.

```{python}
penguins_df.select(
    pl.col("bill_length_mm") / pl.col("bill_depth_mm"),   # → bill_length_mm (!)
    pl.lit(1) + pl.col("year"),                            # → literal
    pl.len(),                                              # → len, broadcast
).head(2)
```

Rule 1 plus rule 5 means a summary that works in dplyr fails in Polars:

```{python}
#| error: true
# summarise(mean(body_mass_g), max(body_mass_g)) works in dplyr
penguins_df.select(pl.col("body_mass_g").mean(), pl.col("body_mass_g").max())
```

Name them:

```{python}
penguins_df.select(
    mass_mean=pl.col("body_mass_g").mean(),
    mass_max=pl.col("body_mass_g").max(),
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Keyword arguments come last

Python puts positional arguments before keyword arguments, so in
`select(pl.col("a"), b=...)` the keyword-named columns always come out last.
If a computed column needs to come first, name it with `.alias()` and pass it
positionally.
:::

### When is a string a column? {#sec-expr-literals}

In R, a bare name is a column and a quoted string is a value. In Polars both
are strings, so Polars decides from **where** the string appears:

| Where the string appears | Read as | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb arguments that name columns | column | `select("x")`, `sort("x")`, `group_by("g")`, `drop("x")` |
| Inputs to expression functions | **column** | `.then("big")`, `.otherwise(...)`, `pl.coalesce("a", "b")`, `pl.concat_str("a", "b")` |
| The right-hand side of an operator | value | `pl.col("species") == "Gentoo"` |
| Parameters that take a value | value | `fill_null("unknown")`, `is_in(["Dream"])`, `str.contains("^B")` |
| Wrapped in `pl.lit()` | value | `pl.lit("big")` |

: String interpretation by position {.striped}

```{python}
#| error: true
penguins_df.select(pl.coalesce("sex", "unknown"))      # looks for a column "unknown"
```

```{python}
penguins_df.select(pl.coalesce("sex", pl.lit("unknown"))).unique(maintain_order=True)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb

If a string is meant as data, wrap it in `pl.lit()`. That is never wrong.
:::

### Parallel, not sequential {#sec-expr-parallel}

All expressions in one context read the **input frame**, independently and in
parallel. The overview shows the loud version of this: a new column cannot
be referenced in the same call. The quiet version is worse. If you replace a
column and then read it in the same call, you get the **old** values:

```r
tibble(a = 1:2) |> mutate(a = a * 10, b = a + 1)   # b = 11, 21 (sees the new a)
```

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}).with_columns(
    pl.col("a") * 10,
    b=pl.col("a") + 1,          # reads the ORIGINAL a → 2, 3
)
```

```text
dplyr  mutate():       a = a * 10  ──►  b = a + 1       sequential: each sees the previous
Polars with_columns(): input ──┬──►  a * 10             parallel: each sees the input
                               └──►  a + 1
```

To get dplyr's behaviour, either chain a second `.with_columns()`, or, if the
intermediate value is only a step toward the result, keep it in a Python
variable:

```{python}
mass_kg = pl.col("body_mass_g") / 1000

penguins_df.select(
    "species",
    mass_kg=mass_kg,
    mass_kg_sq=mass_kg**2,
).head(3)
```

`mass_kg` appears twice in the query, but the lazy optimizer computes it only
once (common-subexpression elimination). In the plan below,
`__POLARS_CSER_…` is the shared subexpression, computed once in
`WITH_COLUMNS` and read twice (more in the [Lazy API](../scale/lazy.qmd)
chapter):

```{python}
print(
    penguins_df.lazy()
    .select("species", mass_kg=mass_kg, mass_kg_sq=mass_kg**2)
    .explain()
)
```

## Where it bites {#sec-expr-gotchas}

| tidyverse behaviour | Polars behaviour |
|---|---|
| bare names are captured implicitly | `pl.col()` builds an explicit `Expr` |
| `mutate()` arguments run in order | expressions in one context run in parallel on the input |
| `summarise()` expects size 1 (more rows → `reframe()`) | `agg()` keeps one row per group and wraps longer results in a list |
| an unnamed output is named after its code (`mean(x)`) | named after its leftmost input (`x`), so duplicates raise an error |
| a quoted string is a value | a string is usually a column name; use `pl.lit()` |
| `arrange()` reorders whole rows | `.sort()` on an expression reorders only that column |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### `sort()` on an expression breaks row alignment {#sec-expr-sort-trap}

```{python}
penguins_df.select(
    "species",
    pl.col("body_mass_g").sort(descending=True, nulls_last=True),
).head(3)
```

The three heaviest penguins are Gentoos, yet these rows say Adelie. The output
has the right length, so nothing raised an error: the masses were sorted and
the species were not. `.unique()`, `.filter()` and `.drop_nulls()` cause the
same misalignment when they happen to produce matching lengths (for example,
two `.unique()` columns of 3 values each); otherwise they raise a `ShapeError`.

**Rule:** to reorder or remove *rows*, use frame verbs (`df.sort()`,
`df.filter()`, `df.unique()`). Use expression-level `sort` / `filter` /
`unique` inside `agg()`, or on a column you select on its own.

```{python}
penguins_df.sort("body_mass_g", descending=True, nulls_last=True).select(
    "species", "body_mass_g"
).head(3)
```

### Python's `and`, `or`, `not`, `in`, `is`

These Python keywords can't be overridden for expressions. Each one asks an
expression for a single `True`/`False`, which an expression can't provide:

```{python}
#| error: true
penguins_df.filter(3000 < pl.col("body_mass_g") < 4000)   # = (3000 < x) and (x < 4000)
```

`is None` is worse, because it does not raise an error. `is` checks Python
object identity before Polars sees anything, so `pl.col("sex") is None`
evaluates to plain `False`, and `filter(False)` keeps no rows:

```{python}
penguins_df.filter(pl.col("sex") is None).height   # 0, silently wrong
```

```{python}
penguins_df.filter(pl.col("sex").is_null()).height   # 11
```

`pl.col("sex") == None` is not right either: comparing with null gives null,
so it also keeps 0 rows (Polars at least warns).

| R | Python habit (wrong) | Polars |
|---|---|---|
| `x > 1 & x < 5` | `1 < x < 5`, `... and ...` | `(x > 1) & (x < 5)` or `x.is_between(1, 5)` |
| `x | y` | `x or y` | `x | y` |
| `!x` | `not x` | `~x` |
| `is.na(x)` | `x is None`, `x == None` | `x.is_null()` |
| `x %in% c("a", "b")` | `x in ["a", "b"]` | `x.is_in(["a", "b"])` |

: Here `x` means an expression such as `pl.col("x")` {.striped}

## Recipes {#sec-expr-recipes}

**Share of total and deviation from the group mean** (aggregations
broadcast inside `with_columns()`):

```{python}
penguins_df.with_columns(
    mass_share=pl.col("body_mass_g") / pl.col("body_mass_g").sum(),
    mass_vs_species=pl.col("body_mass_g") - pl.col("body_mass_g").mean().over("species"),
).select("species", "body_mass_g", "mass_share", "mass_vs_species").head(3)
```

**Conditional aggregation** (≈ `mean(body_mass_g[sex == "female"])`):

```{python}
penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg(
    female_mass=pl.col("body_mass_g").filter(pl.col("sex") == "female").mean(),
    male_mass=pl.col("body_mass_g").filter(pl.col("sex") == "male").mean(),
)
```

**Extract a single value** (≈ `pull()` on a one-cell summary):

```{python}
penguins_df.select(pl.col("body_mass_g").mean()).item()
```

**Build expressions in a loop** (≈ `across()` over a vector of names). Every
context accepts a list of expressions:

```{python}
measures = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm"]

penguins_df.group_by("species", maintain_order=True).agg(
    [pl.col(m).mean().alias(f"{m}_mean") for m in measures]
)
```

[Selectors](selectors.qmd) does the same thing without a loop. Functions that
*return* expressions (the Polars version of `{{ }}`) are in the cheatsheet's
[Programming with Polars](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-programming).
